newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/OEX activity slow, eyes on bonds.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/OEX activity slow, eyes on bonds.

text.p: Activity in U.S. stock index options was very light in cautious morning trade as the broader market bounced from Monday's losses while the technology sector continued sliding, traders said.
"The market's making decent gains, but it's been very choppy lately," one brokerage trader at the Chicago Board Options Exchange said.

Traders attributed the low volume partly to the U.S. Treasury's auction of two-year notes today and five-year notes on Wednesday, noting that interest rates could be the most important factor for the stock market in the weeks to come.

Traders said the broader market seemed to be building up enough strength to go higher without help from the technology sector, a main engine of its tremendous bull run in recent years, and that focus could be shifting to interest rates.

"A favorable climate in the bond market will provide a good backdrop for stocks," said Richard Scarlata, editor of analytical publication Sutton Advisory Letter, who expected the fresh T-note supplies to be digested without much trouble.
"Compared to recent volatility, I think we will begin to be less volatile on a day-to-day basis as confidence returns to the marketplace," he added.

May 740 puts and May 740 calls were the most heavily traded S&P100 index .OEX options on the Chicago Board Options Exchange, with turnover of about 4,600 and 2,800 contracts respectively by 1115 CDT/1615 GMT.
The CBOE volatility index, which reflects implied volatilities of near-month OEX options, was up 0.12 point to 21.29 at 1115 CDT despite a 4.62 point rise in OEX to 746.95.

Volatilities appeared to be pricing in concerns over tech stocks and were less worrisome than in some recent occasions when the VIX slipped below 20, said Todd Salamone, an analyst at Cincinnati-based Investment Research Institute.
"Compared to the last month or so, they're about in line with what they've been," he said. "Nothing really sticky."

Salamone added that the market would probably be able to shrug off the weakness in technology stocks, given the leadership provided by some defensive stocks like pharmaceuticals and a few others like the oil sector.
"That's where money has been heading," he said, adding that those sectors had considerable weight in major indices. "We do not think a rally in tech stocks is needed for the overall market to rally."
Salamone also said bonds and stocks had more to gain than lose from the T-note auctions this week.
"We still view it as a low-expectation environment, which implies there is more room to the upside," he said.
Scarlata added that 7.0 percent in the benchmark bond yield, which currently stands near 7.08 percent, might be a watershed level.
"We're still not out of danger in terms of competition for stocks from bonds," he said. "But if bond yields fall below seven percent, confidence will be restored in the stock market."
